script.opening: “The nurse rang and said one of my blood results needs talking about. I’ve waited years for this, so if you’re going to say my dose has to come down, I’m going to struggle.”

facts.text: Two years on testosterone injections from the NHS gender service, now prescribed by the practice. Three months ago he started having the injections more often than prescribed, “because I felt flat at the end of each cycle”. Has not told anyone.

Headaches for a few weeks, flushed face. No chest pain, no breathlessness, no leg swelling, no visual disturbance, no weakness or numbness. Snores loudly according to Kieran; sometimes wakes up gasping.
Smokes 10 a day. Drinks little water at work (warehouse). Alcohol weekends. Gym three times a week.

facts.topic: Only if asked about relationships or sexual health
facts.text: New partner, Kieran (a cis man), for a month. Vaginal sex without condoms several times, most recently last night. “I can’t get pregnant on T — my periods stopped.” No previous STI tests.
No periods for about 20 months. Has not done a pregnancy test. Does not want a pregnancy. Would be frightened to be pregnant.
Never invited. Did not know he could have one. Anxious about examinations but would consider a self-sample if offered locally.

Defensive about the dose at first. Relaxes if the doctor uses his name and pronouns, explains the risk clearly and says testosterone will not simply be stopped. Shocked to learn testosterone is not contraception; then practical and keen to act.

ice.ideas: “My blood is a bit thick from the T, but that’s normal for guys.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: unprotected sex with his new partner in the belief that testosterone is contraception; also fear of losing his testosterone or being treated as ‘not a real man’ by the system.
ice.expectations: “Keep my dose the same, and keep this quick.”

cues: “Nobody’s touching my dose” — fear of losing treatment; reassure about the process.
Self-increased injection frequency — a cause of the result, to explore without blame.
Snoring and waking up gasping — possible sleep apnoea contributing to erythrocytosis.
A new partner mentioned in passing — open the sexual-health and contraception conversation.

Interprets the result: haematocrit 0.55 on testosterone is above the shared-care action threshold and raises the risk of thrombosis and stroke; asks about symptoms of hyperviscosity and thrombosis
Explores contributing factors without blame: self-adjusted dosing, smoking, possible obstructive sleep apnoea, dehydration

Follows the shared-care agreement: repeat the test, contact the gender service about dose or interval, advise taking injections as prescribed, smoking cessation support, hydration, and assessment for sleep apnoea
Asks respectfully about relationships, sexual practices and contraception, and identifies unprotected vaginal sex with a cis male partner, most recently last night

Explains that testosterone is not a contraceptive and can harm a developing pregnancy; offers emergency contraception (a copper IUD is most effective; levonorgestrel or ulipristal are suitable and testosterone does not interact; check the SPC), a pregnancy test now and 3 weeks after the last unprotected sex
Plans ongoing contraception without oestrogen (copper IUD, LNG-IUS, implant or injection), an STI screen, and offers cervical screening as he has a cervix
Safety-nets for thrombosis and stroke symptoms and for a positive pregnancy test (stop testosterone and seek urgent advice), and arranges follow-up of the repeat result

worked.txt: “Sam, I know how long you waited for testosterone. My aim isn’t to take it away. It’s to keep you safe on it. Can I explain what the result means?”
“Testosterone makes the body produce more red blood cells. Yours have gone up to a level where the blood can get thick, which raises the chance of clots and strokes. It’s fixable.”

“Lots of people adjust their injections to feel steadier. Thanks for telling me. Taking it more often is the most likely reason for the jump, so let’s talk to the gender team about a safer way to even out the levels.”
“You mentioned Kieran. I ask everyone about sexual health and contraception. What kind of sex are you having, and are you using anything?”
“Testosterone stops periods, but it doesn’t reliably stop ovulation, so pregnancy is possible. And testosterone can harm a developing baby, which is why contraception really matters.”

“Because you had sex last night, emergency contraception today is important. A copper coil is the most effective and also works as ongoing contraception. A pill is also fine with testosterone. Let’s do a pregnancy test today and again in three weeks.”

f.learning: Testosterone therapy in trans men commonly raises haemoglobin and haematocrit (erythrocytosis), which increases the risk of thrombosis and stroke. Shared-care protocols from NHS gender services set monitoring and action thresholds; a haematocrit above about 0.54 usually prompts repeating the test, looking for contributing factors and contacting the gender service about dose or interval adjustment, rather than stopping testosterone. Contributing factors include supratherapeutic or self-adjusted dosing, smoking, obstructive sleep apnoea, dehydration and lung disease. RCGP guidance describes the GP’s role as working with specialist gender services, including prescribing and monitoring under shared care. Respectful care means using the person’s name and pronouns and recognising how much treatment matters to them. The hidden agenda is a common, dangerous myth: testosterone does not reliably suppress ovulation, so trans men with a uterus who have vaginal sex with partners who produce sperm can become pregnant, and testosterone can harm a developing pregnancy. CoSRH guidance advises non-oestrogen methods for people using testosterone: copper IUD, LNG-IUS, progestogen-only implant or injection (and the progestogen-only pill). Emergency contraception options are the same as for anyone else; a copper IUD is the most effective, and oral levonorgestrel or ulipristal acetate can be used, with no interaction with testosterone (check the SPC). Arrange a pregnancy test now and 3 weeks after the last unprotected sex, offer an STI screen, and if pregnant, stop testosterone and seek urgent advice. People registered as male are not automatically invited for cervical screening; anyone with a cervix aged 25–64 should be offered it.

Supratherapeutic or self-adjusted dosing, smoking, obstructive sleep apnoea, dehydration, chronic lung disease. Ask about headache, visual symptoms and thrombosis.
Working with the specialist gender service under shared care, as with other specialties; prescribing and monitoring per the agreement [2].
Amenorrhoea on testosterone does not mean no ovulation. Pregnancy is possible, and testosterone can harm a developing pregnancy [3].

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Clarke. Can I check I’ve got your name right, Sam? And it’s he and him?
Yes, thanks. The nurse rang and said one of my blood results needs talking about. I’ve waited years for this, so if you’re going to say my dose has to come down, I’m going to struggle.
I know how long you waited, Sam. My aim isn’t to take testosterone away, it’s to keep you safe on it. Can I explain what we found?

Testosterone makes the body produce more red blood cells. Your level has risen to a point where the blood can get thicker, which raises the chance of clots and strokes. It’s fixable, but we need to act on it.
model.why: Explains the result and its risk

model.text: Right. I thought thick blood was just normal for guys on T.

It goes up a bit for everyone, but yours has jumped since last year. Have you had headaches, a red face, blurred vision, chest pain, breathlessness, a painful swollen leg, or any weakness or numbness?
Headaches, a few weeks. Bit flushed. Nothing else.
How are you taking your injections at the moment?
(pause) A bit more often than it says. I felt flat at the end of each cycle.

Thanks for being honest. Lots of people do that. It’s probably the main reason for the jump, and there are safer ways to even out the levels, which the gender team can advise on. Do you smoke? And has anyone said you snore or stop breathing at night?
Ten a day. And my boyfriend, Kieran, says I snore and sometimes gasp.
That’s useful, I’ll come back to the snoring. You mentioned Kieran. I ask everyone about sexual health and contraception. What kind of sex are you having, and are you using any contraception?
Vaginal sex. No condoms. I can’t get pregnant on T, my periods stopped two years ago.

That’s a really common belief, so I’m glad we’re talking. Testosterone stops periods, but it doesn’t reliably stop ovulation, so pregnancy is possible. And testosterone can harm a developing baby. When did you last have sex?
Last night. And a few times this month. Oh no.
How are you feeling hearing that?
Scared. I don’t want to be pregnant. I just want to be left alone to be me.

Let’s deal with today first. Because of last night, emergency contraception is important. A copper coil fitted within five days is the most effective, and it would also be your ongoing contraception without hormones that affect your T. If you’d rather not have a coil, an emergency pill works with testosterone. Let’s also do a pregnancy test today, and again three weeks after last night.
I’ll take the pill today. I’ll think about the coil.

Good. I’ll also offer a sexual health screen, and longer term the options without oestrogen are the copper coil, the hormonal coil, the implant or the injection. And because you have a cervix, you’re eligible for cervical screening even though you won’t get invitations. We can talk about that when you’re ready.
model.why: STI screen; non-oestrogen contraception; cervical screening

model.text: For the blood result: take the injections as prescribed, I’ll repeat the test in a few weeks and contact the gender team about adjusting the dose or timing so you don’t feel flat. Cutting down smoking would help a lot, and I can refer you to the stop smoking service. Drink plenty of water at work. And I’d like to assess the snoring for sleep apnoea, which can push the blood count up too.
Can you tell me the plan back?
Morning-after pill today, pregnancy test today and in three weeks. Injections as prescribed. Repeat bloods, you’ll talk to the gender team. Think about the coil. Smoking help. Sleep test.

Exactly. If you get sudden weakness, numbness, face drooping, speech or vision problems, chest pain, breathlessness or a painful swollen leg, call 999. If any pregnancy test is positive, stop the testosterone and contact me the same day.

social.t: After years waiting for gender services, fear of losing treatment can make people defensive. Saying early that the aim is safety helps.
The belief that testosterone prevents pregnancy is common and spreads through peer networks.

legal.t: The GP prescribes and monitors under the agreement and should contact the specialist service when results fall outside set limits (RCGP 2024).
Gender reassignment is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010. Care should be respectful and non-discriminatory.

professional.t: Use the person’s chosen name and pronouns and anatomical terms they are comfortable with.
Registered gender affects automatic invitations. Practices should identify people with a cervix (or breast tissue) who may need screening.

community.t: Can fit copper IUDs for emergency contraception, test for STIs and offer inclusive care.
Smoking cessation reduces erythrocytosis and cardiovascular risk.

Chest pain, breathlessness, painful swollen leg: thrombosis, same-day or 999
Positive pregnancy test on testosterone: stop testosterone, urgent advice

playbook.diagnosisLay: “Testosterone tells the bone marrow to make more red cells. Too many make the blood thicker, like syrup, which can clot more easily.”

management.psychosocial: Affirming care; respect his decision about the coil; support around anxiety with examinations.

pitfalls.intro: The result is a protocol action. The marks are in keeping Sam on side, finding the self-adjusted dosing, and uncovering a pregnancy risk he does not know he has.

items.fail: Misgendering or leading with stopping testosterone.
items.why: Trust collapses and he will not disclose.
items.fix: Name and pronouns; say early that the aim is safety.

items.fail: Not asking how he takes his injections.
items.why: Self-adjusted dosing is the likely cause.
items.fix: Ask openly and thank him for honesty.

items.fail: Not liaising with the gender service.
items.why: Dose changes sit within the shared-care agreement.
items.fix: Repeat the test and contact the service.

items.why: Unprotected sex last night needs emergency contraception.
items.fix: Ask respectfully, as with any patient.

items.why: Pregnancy is possible and testosterone can harm a pregnancy.
items.fix: Correct the myth; EC, pregnancy tests, ongoing non-oestrogen method.

items.fail: Forgetting smoking, sleep apnoea and screening.
items.why: They contribute to risk or are missed by registration.
items.fix: Address each briefly with a plan.

Respectful questions; unprotected vaginal sex, last night; myth corrected; feelings.
EC today; pregnancy tests; STI screen; non-oestrogen contraception; cervical screening; repeat bloods and gender service; smoking; OSA.
Teach-back; 999 symptoms; stop T if pregnant.

wordPics.fail: Misgenders Sam; stops testosterone or ignores the result; never asks about sex or contraception, so the risk of pregnancy is missed.
wordPics.pass: Explains the raised haematocrit and plans a repeat with the gender service, identifies unprotected sex and offers emergency contraception and a pregnancy test.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: affirming throughout; explores self-adjusted dosing without blame; addresses smoking and possible sleep apnoea; corrects the testosterone-as-contraception myth clearly; offers a copper IUD as the most effective EC and ongoing method; STI and cervical screening; clear safety-net including stopping testosterone if pregnant.

avoid.dont: “Your blood is too thick, so we’ll have to stop the testosterone.”
avoid.instead: “We’ll repeat it and work with the gender team on the dose, so you stay safe on it.”
avoid.why: The protocol is to adjust and address causes; stopping is rarely needed and harms trust.

avoid.dont: (Assuming no pregnancy risk) skipping sexual history.
avoid.instead: “I ask everyone about sex and contraception. What kind of sex are you having?”

avoid.dont: “Have you thought about going back on the pill?”
avoid.instead: “Options without oestrogen are the coils, the implant and the injection.”
avoid.why: Oestrogen-containing methods are generally avoided with testosterone.

Positive pregnancy test: stop testosterone, contact the practice the same day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The result is a protocol action. The marks are in keeping Sam on side, finding the self-adjusted dosing, and uncovering a pregnancy risk he does not know he has.

items.fail: Misgendering or leading with stopping testosterone.
items.why: Trust collapses and he will not disclose.
items.fix: Name and pronouns; say early that the aim is safety.

items.fail: Not asking how he takes his injections.
items.why: Self-adjusted dosing is the likely cause.
items.fix: Ask openly and thank him for honesty.

items.fail: Not liaising with the gender service.
items.why: Dose changes sit within the shared-care agreement.
items.fix: Repeat the test and contact the service.

items.why: Unprotected sex last night needs emergency contraception.
items.fix: Ask respectfully, as with any patient.

items.why: Pregnancy is possible and testosterone can harm a pregnancy.
items.fix: Correct the myth; EC, pregnancy tests, ongoing non-oestrogen method.

items.fail: Forgetting smoking, sleep apnoea and screening.
items.why: They contribute to risk or are missed by registration.
items.fix: Address each briefly with a plan.
